MUJAHID:v2p689/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p689/r1.speaker: قتادة
MUJAHID:v2p689/r1.claim: Qatada says they went out with firm resolve and purpose.

MUQATIL:68:17-27/r8.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:68:17-27/r8.speaker: author
MUQATIL:68:17-27/r8.claim: They went in severe resolve, thinking themselves capable of controlling their garden.

MAJAZ:v2p265/r3.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p265/r3.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p265/r3.claim: ʿAlā ḥardin can mean withholding, like a she-camel that has no milk.

MAJAZ:v2p265/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p265/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p265/r4.claim: Another interpretation of ʿalā ḥardin is with intention or purpose, supported by an anonymous poem.

MAJAZ:v2p265/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p265/r5.speaker: الأشهب بن رميلة
MAJAZ:v2p265/r5.claim: Al-Ashhab ibn Rumaylah explains ʿalā ḥardin as being in anger.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p309/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p309/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p309/r2.claim: Qatada says they went out with firm resolve; Hasan instead says they went out in hardship or need.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r1.claim: Ḥard means prevention; the word also describes a year with no rain or a she-camel with no milk.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r2.claim: Ḥard can instead mean intent or purpose, as an unnamed poet uses it in a line about pursuing a goal.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r3.speaker: شاعر
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r3.claim: An unnamed poet uses ḥard in a line about pursuing one's aim, supporting the sense “purpose.”

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r4.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r4.speaker: الأشهب بن رميلة
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r4.claim: Al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla uses ḥard in a verse about lions meeting, attesting the noun's usage.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r5.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r5.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r5.claim: The phrase ʿalā ḥard has two dialect pronunciations, like al-darak and al-darak.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r6.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r6.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p479#4/r6.claim: Qādirīn means that they withheld while capable and possessing the means.

TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads ḥard as having ability or power within themselves.

TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r5.claim: Mujāhid says they went with seriousness and felt able to carry out their plan.

TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r6.claim: Al-Ḥasan glosses ḥard as effort or seriousness.

TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r7.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r7.claim: Qatāda says they hurried toward their garden, confident in their ability.

TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r8.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v23p175#2/r8.claim: Ibn Zayd likewise interprets ḥard as serious purpose and confidence in their ability.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r1.claim: Mujāhid says the brothers shared their father’s crop and resolved not to feed the poor until they knew its yield.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r2.claim: Mujāhid says they had already settled on their plan together.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r3.claim: Mujāhid also glosses ḥard as a matter settled by agreement.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r4.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r4.claim: ʿIkrima likewise interprets ḥard as an agreed and settled plan.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r5.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r5.claim: Al-Ḥasan offers poverty or need as another meaning of ḥard.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r6.speaker: سفيان
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r6.claim: Sufyān reads ḥard as anger and cites Ashhab ibn Rumayla’s verse about two lions drinking blood in anger.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r7.speaker: بعض أهل المعرفة بكلام العرب
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r7.claim: Some Basran specialists suggest ḥard means withholding, connecting it with a rainless year or a camel without milk.

TAB-FULL:v23p178/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r8.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v23p178/r8.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the withholding interpretation has no known early authority, although it has a possible linguistic basis.

TAB-FULL:v23p179/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p179/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v23p179/r1.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers that they went toward the garden with an agreed, intended, concealed plan, capable in their own estimation; ḥard commonly means to aim toward something.

TAB-FULL:v23p179/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p179/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v23p179/r2.claim: A rajaz line uses ḥarada for heading toward a destination, supporting the preferred sense of deliberate purpose.

ZAJJAJ:v5p207/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p207/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p207/r3.claim: Ḥard is linked to a year withholding its yield; another interpretation takes it as anger.

ZAJJAJ:v5p207/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p207/r4.speaker: الشاعر
ZAJJAJ:v5p207/r4.claim: An anonymous poetic line uses ḥard to mean setting out toward or aiming for a fertile garden.

NAHHAS:v5p11/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p11/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p11/r3.claim: The strongest explanation of ḥardin is deliberate intent; Mujāhid says they planned it together and thought they could do it.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r10.speaker: معمر عن الحسن
THALABI:v10p16#2/r10.claim: Hasan, as transmitted by Maʿmar, interprets ḥard as need or poverty.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r11.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p16#2/r11.claim: An unnamed interpretation takes ḥard as strength.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r12.speaker: سفيان
THALABI:v10p16#2/r12.claim: Sufyan reads ḥard as anger, supported by a poem describing two black snakes drinking each other's blood in anger.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p16#2/r13.claim: The poem by al-Ashhab ibn Ramlah uses ḥard to mean anger or rage.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r14.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p16#2/r14.claim: Ḥard has two dialectal vowel forms, as with the paired forms darak and darak.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r15.speaker: أبو عبيدة والقتيبي
THALABI:v10p16#2/r15.claim: Abu Ubayda and al-Qutaybi define ḥard as withholding; related Arabic usage describes a rainless year or a she-camel without milk.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r16.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r16.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p16#2/r16.claim: A cited poem uses ḥāradt for a she-camel that has no milk, illustrating the sense of withholding.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r17.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r17.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p16#2/r17.claim: Another interpretation takes ḥard as setting out with intent, illustrated by two lines of rajaz poetry.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p16#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas takes ḥard as their ability or capacity to carry out the plan.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r8.speaker: أبو العالية والحسن
THALABI:v10p16#2/r8.claim: Abu al-Aliya and Hasan read ḥard as earnestness and effort.

THALABI:v10p16#2/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p16#2/r9.speaker: النخعي والقرطبي ومجاهد وعكرمة
THALABI:v10p16#2/r9.claim: These authorities interpret ḥard as a shared, settled plan they had agreed upon.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r12.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r12.claim: حرد can mean seriousness or resolve.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r13.speaker: أبو عبيدة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r13.claim: حرد can mean prevention or withholding.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r14.speaker: الشاعر
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r14.claim: A poem uses حرد for intending or directing oneself toward something.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r16.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r16.speaker: سفيان
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r16.claim: حرد can mean eagerness or greed.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r18.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r18.speaker: السدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r18.claim: حرد can mean anger, or it may be the name of a village.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r19.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r19.speaker: الشعبي
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r19.claim: Being capable may mean having power over the poor.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r20.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r20.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r20.claim: Being capable may mean that they thought themselves able to control their garden.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r21.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r21.speaker: ابن بحر
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r21.claim: Being capable may mean arriving at the garden at the time they had planned.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r22.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r22.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p68/r22.claim: A further reading is that someone powerful relies on wealth and helpers, but when wealth disappears the helpers disperse and he becomes unable and disobeyed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r10.speaker: الأعشى
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r10.claim: Al-Aʿsha's line uses حاردت for a she-camel withholding milk, illustrating the sense of prevention.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r11.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r11.claim: حرد can also mean aiming or setting out toward a goal, as illustrated by a Hudhali poet's description of a torrent.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r12.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r12.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r12.claim: Abu Ubayd cites poetry using أحردت حردي as another attestation of the word's lexical sense.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r8.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r8.claim: Abu Ishaq says they set out very early at the time they had fixed for their wrongful harvest.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p100#2/r9.claim: حرد has multiple lexical senses, including prevention or withholding, as in a year with little rain and a she-camel withholding milk.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says they thought themselves capable of taking their garden's produce; Muqatil and the exegetes agree.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r2.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r2.claim: Abu Ishaq says they considered themselves able to reach their garden without any calamity stopping them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r3.speaker: ابن قتيبة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p104/r3.claim: Ibn Qutayba says they were prevented despite being capable, with capability here meaning possession of wealth and means.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:68:22-27/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:68:22-27/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:68:22-27/r4.claim: They went with firm purpose, believing they had power over the garden's fruit.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r1.speaker: أبو العالية ومجاهد وقتادة وابن زيد
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r1.claim: They take ḥardin as purposeful seriousness and exertion in what the owners intended.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r2.speaker: الحسن
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r2.claim: Hasan explains ḥardin as the strain of poverty.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r3.speaker: سفيان
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r3.claim: Sufyan takes ḥardin to mean anger.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة والقتبي
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r4.claim: They understand it as firm intent to withhold, supported by idioms for a year withholding rain and camels withholding milk.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r5.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والقرظي والنخعي
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r5.claim: They interpret it as a matter resolved by common agreement.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says they thought themselves powerful and able.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r7.claim: Another view takes it as setting out purposefully, from the idiom ḥarada ḥardahu, to aim at his aim.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r8.speaker: السدي
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r8.claim: Al-Suddi says ḥard is the name of the garden, but the commentator judges this explanation unsound.

JISHUMI:v10p7034/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7034/r9.claim: Qādirīn may mean that they thought they could keep the poor away, or that they expected to reach the garden at their chosen harvest time; the latter is Abu Muslim's view.

JISHUMI:v10p7036/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7036/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7036/r4.claim: The poor had an enforceable due in the harvest, variously identified as a tenth or as the fruit that fell during picking.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r2.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وأبو العالية
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r2.claim: They read حرد as acting with earnestness and effort.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r3.speaker: القرظي ومجاهد وعكرمة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r3.claim: They understand حرد as a firm, jointly settled plan, a sense of purpose and determination.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة والقتيبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r4.claim: They intended to bar the poor; Arabic also describes a year without rain or a camel without milk as حارد.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r5.speaker: الشعبي وسفيان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r5.claim: They went out angry at the poor.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p196/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says they thought they were able to control their garden and fruit, with no one able to stop them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r10.claim: حرد can also mean anger; the author cites al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla's verse about snakes drinking blood in anger.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r11.claim: قادرين may mean capable, as they believed themselves to be, or measuring out and restricting the poor.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r12.claim: The restriction sense of قدر is illustrated by 65:7, where a person's provision is made narrow.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r6.claim: حرد may mean withholding or preventing, as when camels give little milk or a barren year produces no crop.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r7.speaker: الكميت
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r7.claim: Al-Kumayt's verse uses حاردت for an unproductive, withholding season.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r8.speaker: بعض اللغويين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r8.claim: Some lexicographers explain حرد as heading toward a purpose, citing a rajaz line about a flood moving toward its source.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r9.speaker: القرطبي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p349#3/r9.claim: Al-Qurtubi cites a poem in which حرد means to aim for or pursue something.

TABRISI:68:17-33/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:68:17-33/r10.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة وأبي العالية
TABRISI:68:17-33/r10.claim: Alternatively, ‘with resolve’ means they went in earnest and with determination.

TABRISI:68:17-33/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:68:17-33/r11.speaker: أبي عبيدة
TABRISI:68:17-33/r11.claim: Another view takes it as determined to prevent the poor.

TABRISI:68:17-33/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:68:17-33/r12.speaker: سفيان
TABRISI:68:17-33/r12.claim: Another view says they were angry with the poor.

TABRISI:68:17-33/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:68:17-33/r13.speaker: أبو مسلم
TABRISI:68:17-33/r13.claim: Alternatively, they thought themselves able to reach the garden at the time they had planned to cut its crop.

TABRISI:68:17-33/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:68:17-33/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:68:17-33/r9.claim: They set out intending to keep the poor away, believing they could prevent them and retain the garden's produce.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r10.speaker: الشعبي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r10.claim: Alternatively, they believed themselves able to keep the poor away.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r11.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r11.claim: Alternatively, they were withholding while still possessing the means to give.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r2.claim: Ḥard can mean want or poverty.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r3.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وأبو العالية والفراء ومقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r3.claim: Ḥard can mean seriousness or earnest resolve.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r4.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r4.claim: Ḥard can mean an agreed plan they had prepared together.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r5.speaker: السدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r5.claim: Ḥard may be the name of the garden.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r6.speaker: الشعبي وسفيان
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r6.claim: Ḥard can mean anger at the poor; Abū ʿUbayda cites a line about two tribes meeting in anger and exchanging blood.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r7.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r7.claim: Ḥard can mean withholding, as in a year without rain or a she-camel without milk.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r8.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r8.claim: Ḥard may mean aiming or going toward a destination; they cite a verse about a flood moving toward a garden and note two vowel forms.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r9.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p336#7/r9.claim: They thought themselves able to reach and harvest their garden.

RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r1.claim: Ḥard may mean prevention, as in a year that withholds rain or a she-camel that withholds milk; it can also mean anger, which bars the angry person from being admitted.

RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r2.claim: Another view takes ḥard as purposeful haste; a poem about a rushing flood and the phrase qiṭā ḥirād (swift sandgrouse) support the sense of speed.

RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v30p79#2/r3.claim: A third view treats Ḥard as the proper name of the garden, toward which they hurried, believing they could harvest it and deprive the poor.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r10.speaker: السدي وسفيان
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r10.claim: Al-Suddi and Sufyan interpret hard as anger.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r11.speaker: ابن السكيت
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r11.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit says hard may be vocalized with a fatḥa and describes an angry lion; a verse also uses it for anger.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r12.claim: Another explanation is isolation: hard means withdrawing from one’s people; Hudhayl uses munḥarid for solitary, and al-Azhari says Hard was their village’s name.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas and others explain hard as intention and say the brothers believed they had the ability to carry out their purpose.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r5.claim: Hard means purpose or intention, as in the expression “I intended your intention.”

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r6.speaker: الشاعر الراجز
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r6.claim: A rajaz line compares the brothers’ directed purpose to a flood heading for a fruitful garden; al-Mubarrad says the garden bears produce, while others describe water flowing through its furrows.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r7.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r7.claim: Qatada and Mujahid gloss hard as earnest effort.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r8.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r8.claim: Hasan says it means they were in need and poverty.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة والقتيبي
QURTUBI-FULL:68:23-25/r9.claim: Abu Ubayda and al-Qutaybi say hard means withholding, from the term for camels whose milk has dwindled.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r1.speaker: السدي
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r1.claim: Al-Suddi says Hard was the name of their garden; the word has two pronunciations.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r2.claim: Most readers have the word with a quiescent letter; Abu al-Aliya and Ibn al-Sumayqa read it with fatḥa, both being dialectal forms.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r3.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r3.claim: Al-Farra says qadirin means they had planned and determined their affair.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r4.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r4.claim: Qatada says they considered themselves able to control their garden.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r5.speaker: الشعبي
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r5.claim: Al-Sha‘bi says they thought they were able to keep the poor away.

QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:68:25/r6.claim: Another interpretation is that they had the means to withhold charity but chose to do so.

BAYDAWI-FULL:68:23-25/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:68:23-25/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:68:23-25/r3.claim: They expected to control the harvest but arrived with deprivation: حرد can mean drought or an unyielding animal, and their plan to deprive the poor instead brought deprivation on themselves.

BAYDAWI-FULL:68:23-25/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:68:23-25/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:68:23-25/r4.claim: Other readings explain حرد as their mutual anger, so they could achieve only resentment; it can also mean purpose and speed, supported by a verse describing a flood, or be the garden’s proper name.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p270#5/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p270#5/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p270#5/r1.claim: Ḥard may mean determination to prevent the poor, or direction and speed; it may also name the orchard itself.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r2.speaker: أبو عبيد والقتبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r2.claim: They explain ḥard as withholding, supported by expressions for camels whose milk dries up and a year with little rain and abundance.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r3.claim: Another meaning of ḥard is anger; Abū Naḍr transmits a light pronunciation and cites a horse poem as evidence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r4.speaker: الأشهب بن رميلة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r4.claim: Al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla's verse uses ḥard for rage, in a description of lions who meet and drink one another's blood.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r5.speaker: ابن السكيت
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r5.claim: Ibn al-Sikkīt permits a vowel variant and gives related usages for anger, fierce lions, and solitary or separated things.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r6.speaker: الأصمعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r6.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says المنحرد means a solitary person in Hudhayl's dialect.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p233/r7.claim: Ḥard can also mean intention or aim, as in a poetic line about a flood heading toward a fruit-laden garden.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p242/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p242/r14.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p242/r14.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says they went with intent and confidence in their own power, rushing to their garden and believing they could harvest it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p242/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p242/r15.speaker: أبو عبيدة والقتبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p242/r15.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and al-Qutaybī interpret ḥard as withholding; they thought they could deny the poor their share, so God denied them the crop.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r1.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r1.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets ḥard as need and want.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r2.speaker: السدي وسفيان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r2.claim: Al-Suddī and Sufyān say it means anger: they had power only to feel rage and resent one another.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r3.claim: Other interpretations are that they were alone, or that Ḥard was their village's or garden's name.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p243/r4.claim: Since قدر can mean making narrow, another possibility is that they intended to restrict the poor, as in God's phrase “whose provision is constrained.”

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r1.claim: ‘Qadirin’ may be a circumstantial accusative from the subject of ‘ghadaw’; ‘ala hard’ may depend on it, or itself be the circumstantial phrase with ‘qadirin’ as a second or nested circumstantial.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r10.speaker: الأزهري
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r10.claim: Al-Azhari says Hard is the name of their village; the author considers both proper-name explanations very remote.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r11.claim: ‘Qadirin’ most plainly means possessing power, though it may instead derive from estimation and mean restricting the poor.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r2.claim: One lexical view takes hard as anger or fury; a line attributed to al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla uses hard for the rage of fighting lions.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r3.claim: An unnamed poet pairs hard with anger, supporting the sense of fury; the source says the two words are coordinated because their wording differs.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r4.claim: Hard may mean withholding or scarcity: camels give little milk and a year little rain; Abu Ubayd and al-Qutaybi report this usage.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r5.claim: The word has several vocalized forms and derivatives, including ‘hardan’ and ‘harid’; Arabic also describes a lion as hard and lions as hawarid.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r6.speaker: الأصمعي
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r6.claim: Hard may mean isolation or withdrawal; the verb can mean to withdraw, and a solitary star is called kawkab hard. Al-Asma‘i identifies the usage as Hudhayli.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r7.claim: Another lexical view is intention or direction: ‘harada yaḥrudu hardaka’ means to intend your direction; a cited verse illustrates the expression.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r8.claim: The verse has been interpreted according to all the listed senses of hard.

SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r9.speaker: السدي
SAMIN-DURR:68:25/r9.claim: Al-Suddi says Hard is the proper name of the owners’ particular garden.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196#2/r1.claim: They thought they had power over their orchard and could carry out their plan.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r4.claim: The phrase “on resolve” can mean strength and severity; other reported meanings are earnestness, anger, hostility toward the poor, or the name of their town, with the last rejected as far-fetched.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r7.speaker: الشعبي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r7.claim: Al-Sha‘bi explains the phrase as resolve against the poor.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r8.speaker: السدي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p196/r8.claim: Al-Suddi says Harad was the name of their village, but Ibn Kathir dismisses this as a distant interpretation.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p105/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p105/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p105/r6.claim: Ḥard can mean aim, intense anger, firm insistence, haste, stinginess, or lack of good, as in a season without rain or a camel withholding milk.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p105/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p105/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p105/r7.claim: They thought themselves capable of harvesting because they had made no exception; such certainty about a future act presumes a power no creature has.

DURR-FULL:v8p251/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p251/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p251/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the owners as having power or ability.

DURR-FULL:v8p252/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p252/r1.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p252/r1.claim: Mujahid says they went out intent on a plan they had settled among themselves: no poor person would enter.

DURR-FULL:v8p252/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p252/r3.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p252/r3.claim: Hasan says they were resolutely set against the poor.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r1.speaker: أبو عبيد وغيره
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r1.claim: They gloss حرد as prevention, drawing on camels whose milk dries up and a year with little rain and fertility.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r2.claim: The prepositional phrase is fronted before قادرين for exclusivity and rhyme: they set out able only to deprive, despite being able to benefit the poor.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r3.claim: On one reading, they sought to deprive the poor but received deprivation themselves; another says their garden was barren, so they lost its benefits.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r4.claim: Alternatively حرد attaches to غدوا and means the garden's barrenness, punning with حرث; capable is mock reversal of their plan to reap and deny the poor.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r5.speaker: أبو نصر أحمد بن حاتم
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r5.claim: Abu Nasr reports حرد with fatḥa as anger and cites a line describing horses filled with rage; they can only anger one another.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r6.speaker: سفيان والسدي
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r6.claim: Sufyan and al-Suddi transmit the interpretation that the brothers could only anger one another, as in their later reproaching each other.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas reports حرد as intention and speed: they hurried toward the garden believing they could reap it.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r8.speaker: الأزهري والسدي
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r8.claim: Al-Azhari calls حرد the name of their village, and al-Suddi gives it as the garden's name; the author doubts this was intended.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p31#3/r9.claim: Other glosses make حرد mean their isolation from the poor or their restriction of the poor from the charity their father gave.

ELMALILI:68:7-33#5/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:68:7-33#5/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:68:7-33#5/r10.claim: Ḥard is read as forceful prevention and despotism: they set out early with power only for greed and anger.

ELMALILI:68:7-33#5/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:68:7-33#5/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:68:7-33#5/r11.claim: Collective speed and despotism can be more powerful and dreadful than an individual's.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r1.claim: وغدوا على حرد قادرين is a circumstantial clause with an implicit قد, describing their state as they set out.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r2.claim: Repeating غدوا in the circumstantial clause makes their ill-fated early departure striking; Ibn al-Qays's verse similarly turns back to the night already described.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r3.speaker: امرؤ القيس
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r3.claim: The quoted verse about spending the night awake illustrates the rhetorical return to an already-mentioned night.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r4.claim: حرد can mean prevention, forceful purpose or speed, or anger.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r5.claim: The word's selection has a rhetorical subtlety because its different meanings attach aptly either to قادرين or to غدوا.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r6.claim: If حرد modifies قادرين, the fronted phrase restricts them to being able to withhold good or fruit, not help anyone; calling this ability is ironic.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r7.claim: If حرد means speed or resolve, it modifies غدوا and describes their energetic haste; قادرين then conveys their mistaken confidence that they could accomplish their aim.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p84/r8.claim: This reading foreshadows their failure, confirmed by their response on seeing the ruined garden and by the preceding calamity.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p85/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p85/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p85/r1.claim: If حرد means anger, the phrase means they could do nothing but rage at the poor, having failed to gather the fruit they sought; the fronting restricts their capacity to anger.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p85/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p85/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p85/r2.claim: Al-Suddi says حرد is the name of their village or orchard; Ibn Ashur suspects this is a contrived explanation drawn from the verbs اغدوا and غدوا.

TABATABAI:68:20-28/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:68:20-28/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:68:20-28/r6.claim: They set out determined to prevent the poor from receiving anything, confidently planning to harvest it all.

BINTSHATI:v2p63/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p63/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p63/r4.claim: Ḥard means withholding or preventing, with an added sense of aversion, as in a year withholding yield or a camel withholding milk.

BINTSHATI:v2p63/r9.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p63/r9.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p63/r9.claim: Exegetes elaborate the garden story: it belonged to a righteous man who left it to his people and town; reports place it in Yemen near Ṣanʿāʾ, Abyssinia, or among the People of Scripture.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p433/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p433/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p433/r6.claim: The word denotes ardor, freshness, resolve, and a hurried gait; their resolve protects them from the poor, while ‘able’ conveys confidence that ripe fruit and their plan face no obstacle.

STUDYQURAN:68:17/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:68:17/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:68:17/r9.claim: Their resolve shows their determination or overconfidence that they could control who received the produce, although only God determines.
